title: The Jesus Prayer
hook: one short line, said over and over, moving from the lips toward the heart

segments.voice: Yesterday, the desert, and Evagrius watching the thoughts like a doctor. Your line was name the thought. Which one kept coming back? Today, a prayer that grew out of that same desert soil. Day one thousand three hundred seventy.

A knotted cord of black wool, looped around a wrist. Each knot is tied in a small cross. An Orthodox Christian moves a thumb from one knot to the next, and with each one says a single line, quietly: Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me. Then the next knot. The same line. On a bus. Waiting for coffee. Lying awake. No new words, no long list of requests. Just that line, again, until it starts to feel less like something said and more like something breathed. Orthodox Christians call it the Jesus Prayer. Today's word is the tradition of stillness it lives in.
screen: `A KNOTTED CORD.` → `ONE LINE, AGAIN AND AGAIN.` → `SAID, THEN BREATHED.`

segments.voice: Hesychasm comes from the Greek hesychia, stillness. It names a way of prayer in Eastern Orthodox Christianity, kept especially by monks, and gathered in a collection of writings called the Philokalia. Four turns. First, the words come from the Gospels. In Luke, a tax collector stands far off and prays, in the old King James wording, "God be merciful to me a sinner." A blind man by the road calls out, "Jesus, thou son of David, have mercy on me." The Jesus Prayer gathers cries like these into one line. Some say it with the words a sinner at the end. Second, the breath. Some writers in the Philokalia describe saying the prayer with the rhythm of breathing, the first half on the in-breath, the second on the out-breath, with the attention resting low, near the heart. Third, the heart. That's your line. Orthodox teachers speak of the prayer moving from the lips, to the mind, to the heart, until it isn't just recited but becomes, as they put it, the prayer of the heart. The heart here means the center of the whole person, not just feelings. Fourth, a caution the tradition gives itself. Orthodox teachers say the breathing methods are a help, not the point, and that this prayer is best learned with a spiritual father or mother, not from a book or an app. For Orthodox Christians this is not a technique for calm. It's speaking to Christ. So for anyone outside that faith, the respectful way in is to listen and learn, the way you'd sit quietly at the back of someone else's church.
screen: `HESYCHIA: STILLNESS.` · `WORDS FROM THE GOSPELS.` · `WITH THE BREATH, TOWARD THE HEART.` · `LEARNED WITH A GUIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: learn about it respectfully. Sit, and let the breath settle. If you pray as a Christian, you can say the Jesus Prayer slowly, the way it's said, without forcing the breath. If you don't, simply sit in the stillness the word hesychia points to. Let the breath come and go on its own. Notice where your attention rests in the body, and let it drift down toward the center of the chest. The bell holds the time.
Hesychasm. From the Greek for stillness: the Orthodox way of prayer in which the Jesus Prayer moves from the lips toward the heart. Today's word.

Your line: the prayer of the heart. Today, once, when you're waiting in line, let your attention drop from your head to the center of your chest for three breaths, and just notice it there. Day one thousand three hundred seventy.

howItsDone: Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer, often with a knotted prayer rope, repeating it quietly through the day, and monks and others who practice hesychasm learn it under the guidance of a spiritual father or mother.

notes: The Jesus Prayer's wording ('Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me') is given in the voice as the traditional prayer, from the index; it is not quoted from a modern translation. Confirm the form, and the variant ending 'a sinner'.
Breathing method (first half on the in-breath, second on the out-breath, attention near the heart) is a simplified paraphrase of Philokalia writers; confirm.
Lips, mind, heart progression is a common Orthodox teaching (e.g. Theophan the Recluse); not cited to a specific text; confirm.
The caution about learning with a spiritual guide is stated as the tradition's own teaching; confirm.
Practice offers the prayer only to those who pray as Christians and stillness to everyone else; confirm the respectful framing for Orthodox Keepers.
Outline credits the Philokalia; the hook's prayer rope (chotki/komboskini) detail of knots tied as small crosses is general; confirm.
